captions.text: This is fevm-replay.
It runs real Ethereum mainnet transactions inside fevm, the EVM written in Fe,
and checks that each one ends exactly as it did on chain.
115,213 mainnet transactions, and no fevm bug:
every difference was traced to a cause outside the interpreter.
Now the headline:
every root in the header comes out of fevm.
The parent's Merkle proofs are a witness:
fevm runs the block on it,
writes its end state into that partial trie and hashes it again.
That must be the header's state root, as a stateless client checks it.
Every other root must match too.
Here is that run:
block 26,424,805, checked by CI on every push.
71 of 71 transactions match, they re-encode to the transactions root,
the requests hash matches, and the state root is the header's.
Change one withdrawal by one wei, and the withdrawals root,
the end-state proof and the computed state root all fail.
A clean run rests on one 32-byte block hash.
Fe functions declare their effects.
The function that decides match or diff gets a text buffer and nothing else,
so calling the network from it is a type error.
Is a Fe port a drop-in replacement?
Ask mainnet.
The USDT port ran in 21,230 mainnet transactions, and none behaved differently.
DAI's certificate:
10,562 mainnet transactions, 211,240 mutated runs, none different,
all 21 planted mutants caught.
The explorer shows where two runs part:
before its fix, the Fe port reverted on a bot's packed address.
After the fix, they no longer part.
Opcode by opcode, Fe spends 44% less gas than solc on stack shuffling,
but 25% more on memory.
No Fe install needed:
the release binary runs the seven saved mainnet fixtures, and all seven match.
fevm-replay:
mainnet blocks validated statelessly, natively and in your browser, with a light client,
Ethereum's own system code in Fe, and what stateless Ethereum and Glamsterdam would cost.
Code on GitHub, results at fevm-replay.vercel.app.
Three consecutive mainnet blocks, in one run.
Block one:
230 transactions, all matching.
Block two:
Block three:
And the links hold:
each block's parent is the one before it,
its pre-state proven against the state root fevm computed.
Blocks near the chain head, proven and validated as they came.
fevm's own chain layer and geth agree on every one.
This page lists each block, with the witness per transaction and per million gas,
and whose storage weighs the most:
the deeper a contract's storage trie, the more each slot it touches costs.
And what would stateless Ethereum cost?
Priced by the EIP-4762 draft, these blocks would need 25% more gas,
and 39% of transactions would run out of gas at the limit they were sent with.
Exempting the coinbase saves the transfers, but not the contract calls:
23% still fail.
An independent implementation, ethereumjs,
charges the same gas on all 18,967 transactions.
Fe can stand in for Ethereum's own code too.
All four system contracts the protocol calls in every block are ported from assembly.
Here a mainnet block runs its system calls on the Fe ports:
two consolidation requests come out, and every root still matches.
On 85 blocks it held, after catching one bug in our own port.
That is also why the validator compiles to WebAssembly, with fevm inside.
Here it runs in the browser, on a mainnet block with an EIP-7002 withdrawal request:
every root in its header holds, and all 286 transactions match, in about two seconds.
Or pick a block near the head, and the page fetches it from public nodes itself.
And Glamsterdam, the next fork, whose rules fevm already implements?
The same 18,967 transactions, each with the gas limit it was sent with:
6,693 that succeeded would fail, and the rest would use 25% more gas.
Over a thousand are plain transfers to new accounts:
creating an account now costs state gas.
From a terminal, the same module validates a block three behind the head:
223 of 223 transactions match, every root holds.
Its hash is checked as a light client checks it:
from a finalized checkpoint, through Ethereum's sync committee, 511 of 512 signed,
and each signature is verified twice, the second time by fevm's own BLS12-381 precompiles,
written in Fe.
